newsitem.title: CZECH REPUBLIC: Shrine fails to save Czech's home on 75th birthday.
newsitem.headline: Shrine fails to save Czech's home on 75th birthday.

text.p: With the image of Saint Peter looking over his shoulder, Josef Feldvabl stared at the seemingly harmless stream a stone's throw away.
On the banks of the Morava in the eastern Czech Republic, he has lived through Nazi occupation, a Soviet-led invasion and painful retirement in the new capitalism.
But his 75th birthday brought a calamity which could not be blamed on politics.
In a few hours on July 10, the River Morava, which had never before risen even to the retaining wall across the street, filled Feldvabl's two-century-old family home.
He fled and returned when the waters receded, but there wasn't much left.
"What a present," the robust former factory worker said as bulldozers finished off the demolition. "It's a present from God," he added, with a touch of irony but fighting back tears.
In towns and villages up and down this fertile valley -- and across much of Central Europe -- people are trying to dig out and make sense of the devastation from the worst flooding on record.
The wall of water which swept through the region after torrential rains in early July has been responsible for more than 100 deaths in Poland and the Czech Republic.
The floods have destroyed thousands of homes, businesses, and crops, costing billions of dollars in the worst natural disaster this area has known.

In the ancient market town of Uherske Hradiste, waterlogged remnants of homes and belongings are now piled into muddy alleyways. The stench of stagnant water, the drone of bulldozers and bites from swarming mosquitoes add to the misery.
"We had plenty of warning, but nobody would believe it could come up here," Feldvabl said, pointing down at the river.
"I've lived through Hitler, Communism, capitalism," he said. "Do you believe in God?"

At the corner of where Feldvabl's house once stood there is an almost pristine religious shrine. The white column with glass-encased paintings of Saint Peter and the Madonna used to adjoin the building.
The modest one-story home was reduced to rubble, the shrine survived unscathed. A miracle?
"No, just better bricks and cement," said Feldvabl, who throughout his life has maintained the shrine, which was supposed to protect his home.
"I still believe in God, but I don't believe in the saints any more. This was God's will."
He had just repainted in the spring.
For now, Feldvabl is living with grandchildren and trying to figure out what to do.

The local government has provided modest grants to pay for demolition work and to lay a new foundation, but with post-communist budgets tight and a meagre pension paying just enough to live on, finding funds to re-build will be tough.
"Maybe some millionaire will come. There are a lot of millionaires now, you know?"
